quotes.text: As Perfume Genius, Michael Hadreas has long straddled the gap between pop and the avant-garde.

He invites a dozen people into a dusky room filled with all the instruments you can think of, crafting dream-like vignettes wrapped in waves of transcendent noise, jazz, and chamber art: Dada for the 21st Century.
Glory, his fifth album with producer Blake Mills, is a bit looser, more spacious, illustrative of an artist who has learned to balance immersion with some degree of detachment.
Glory reestablishes Hadreas's affinity for pop essentials while giving him a bit more room to express his alt-self.

Songs 3-10 of Glory unfurl seamlessly and complementarily, as Hadreas works with impressionistic lyrics, steamy melodies, and vocals that conjure longing, PTSD (personal and archetypal / processed and unprocessed), and, again, an understated equanimity.

Hadreas alchemizes his elusive lyrics into a palpable manifesto on hurt and redemption, grief and communality, how we're forever alone yet never alone. In this way, he integrates raw confessionalism and sober reportage.
With Glory, Hadreas continues to hone juxtapositions of heaviness and buoyancy, yoking the spacious and the claustrophobic.
More specifically, he explores the dynamics of entanglement and removal, melding objectivity, magical realism, and a literary bent.
Hadreas is certainly a pop songwriter, though he filters his hooks through an epic orientation, viewing the micro or quotidian through mythic lens.
Better known by the pseudonym Perfume Genius, the art pop balladeer is lauded for his heartrending lyrics on love, loss and sexuality — trading genres like pairs of shoes.

Hadreas' 2020 release, Set My Heart on Fire Immediately, is by far the best example of his chameleon-esque variability, with the artist bouncing from soaring, electrified ballads to meaty, pounding pop.

Glory, released on Friday, partially continues this trend, but with a much less sprawling sound. Instead, Hadreas embraces an earthy suburbanite rock infused with lush electronics and signature unplaceable melancholy.
Glory further proves that Hadreas is a formidable 21st century rocker, producing quality rootsy rhythms with a dose of pop shine from modest electronics.
Few other songwriters can weave whirling scenes of heartbreak and victimhood into short bursts of pop songcraft, and Glory delivers more stellar tales for his discography.
It's evident that Hadreas leans toward the confines of a short and sweet ballad.
Hadreas's indie music stylistically explores pop and rock with various influences and atmospheres.
The album was a transformative leap for Hadreas and marked a new trajectory in his career.
The album was originally composed as a musical accompaniment for choreographer Kate Wallich's contemporary dance piece The Sun Still Burns Here.
Hadreas's musical style has been described as art pop, indie rock, baroque pop, indie pop, chamber pop, folk, pop, and glam rock.

But music can also be reflective of what an artist seemingly goes through or had gone through and that gives the listeners a stripped down to the point listening experience that functions less like a distraction from all that's going on in life but more as a form of empathy to the listener without the singer even physically being there to provide this feeling of empathy.
I feel he's music is essentially a part of him.
Perfume Genius was a recovering addict who had reached a low point in his life and found comfort in the making of his music.

Whether these characters exist in one universe or are even real and known people in Hadreas's life doesn't take away from the fact that these people don't feel alien. If anything they feel like characters that we can relate to and in some ways are pieces of ourselves and our own anxieties and fears.
Hadreas is able to continue to illustrate these feelings abandonment and having no one.
Throughout the album Hadreas's voice is often in the background which adds to the rustic quality of the album but also add this sense of delicacy to it.
In tracks where the lyrics are not comprehensible (and I'm not saying I don't understand. genius literally has it as '?') Hadreas still gives us these feelings and emotions.
From a music critic perspective I can say that this was such a phenomenal start point for Perfume Genius and his career and albums that came after.

Perfume Genius's sound has evolved by leaps and bounds since then, while still maintaining much of the hushed, intimate, emotionally intense magic that has made Mike's songwriting captivating for the duration of Perfume Genius's run.

I think his music really reached a peak of lushness and beauty and even accessibility when he began working consistently with producer Blake Mills, specifically around the creation of his incredible record, No Shape, which dropped in 2017, I believe.

Even 2022's Ugly Season, which was a pretty peculiar record for the Perfume Genius project, which was delivered like any other album, but originally conceived as a companion to a dance piece. The songwriting on this record took a very in a different shape as a result, I fear.

One of the most key things about this track being that Mike is embracing more guitar this time around. Oh, guitar, which I know is not the most exciting move in the world for a music project to make. But historically, the fuel for the Perfume, Genius fire has been Mike's very unique voice and piano.

I can commend them a little bit, though, for trying to experiment on the following "Capezio", where Mike does try to take a different vocal approach, really leaning into his falsetto this time around.
Because, yeah, a lack of concrete focus and direction musically on these tracks, it just continues to be an Achilles heel throughout the record.
Singer/songwriter whose brutally honest songs range from fragile piano ballads to swaggering glam rock.
